title: As-Sabur, the Most Patient
tomorrow: Jordan asks Dadi: what do you call God when it's just you?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ar-Rashid, the Guide to the Right Path: ask, consult, resolve, then trust. The line: rightly guided. Amira chose. Now comes the part after choosing: waiting.

Moving day. The truck said morning, and it's past lunch. The tape has run out, the phone is nearly dead, and Dadi keeps stopping in each empty room of her apartment, touching the door frame, saying something under her breath. Amira, holding the last box, hears her own voice come out sharp: "Dadi. Can we please just go?" Dadi goes quiet. A sentence like that is out before anyone decides to say it. So what is patience, if it's always one second too late?
screen: `THE TRUCK IS LATE.` → `DADI. CAN WE PLEASE JUST GO?` → `ONE SECOND TOO LATE.`

segments.voice: Today's Name, the last of the traditional ninety-nine, is As-Sabur, the Most Patient. A hadith gives it a startling picture: no one is more patient with hurtful words than Allah. People say He has a son, the hadith says, and still He gives them health and provision. Insulted, and still feeding the one who insults. That's the scale of it. Then a story at human size. The Prophet, peace be upon him, passed a woman weeping at a grave and told her to be mindful of Allah and patient. Not recognizing him, she snapped: leave me alone. When she learned who it was, she came to his door to apologize. He told her: patience is at the first strike. That's the answer to the hook. Patience isn't the calm that arrives an hour later. It's the first second, the one Amira missed. And the woman at the grave missed it too, and she still came back. The Qur'an gives the help for both moments, in Surah al-Baqarah: "Seek help in steadfastness and prayer. Lo! Allah is with the steadfast." Here's the thing to tell a friend: Pickthall's word there, steadfastness, is the same Arabic word as patience, sabr. Patience in this tradition isn't sitting still. It's standing firm.
screen: `NO ONE MORE PATIENT THAN ALLAH.` · `THE WOMAN AT THE GRAVE.` · `PATIENCE IS AT THE FIRST STRIKE.` · `SABR: STEADFAST, STANDING FIRM.` · then, large: `PATIENT.`

segments.voice: Find the most annoying sound near you: a fridge hum, traffic, someone else's video. Listen to it for the whole sit without trying to fix it or leave it. Each time you want to, that's a first strike; stay one more breath.
As-Sabur. The Most Patient, who keeps giving to the very people who wrong Him.
Here is the line: patient, at the first strike, and if you miss it, at the second. Ninety-nine of ninety-nine, complete.

howItsDone: Muslims say inna lillahi wa inna ilayhi raji'un at a sudden loss, often the first words at the first strike, and ask Allah for sabr in du'a.

original.note: Arabic: the Most Patient, the last Name in the traditional list; sabr is patience.

trapdoor: what you thought: patience is waiting quietly in a long line.
what it means: it's the first second, and standing firm; Allah's own patience keeps giving to those who wrong Him.

Hadiths paraphrased: Bukhari 7378 / Muslim 2804 (patience with hurtful words; 'no one is more patient' is the hadith's own superlative) and Bukhari 1283 / Muslim 926 (the woman at the grave). Confirm numbers and wording.
Qur'an 2:153 quoted from Pickthall 1930; confirm exact wording. 'Steadfastness' there renders sabr (ista'inu bi-s-sabr); confirm.
'The last of the traditional ninety-nine': as-Sabur closes the list in Tirmidhi 3507; the count 99 comes from the hadith of the ninety-nine Names (Bukhari 2736). Confirm the claim is acceptable.
'If you miss it, at the second' (carry) is drawn from the woman returning to apologize; it is a reading, not a hadith statement. Confirm it's fair.
The woman at the grave is grieving; told gently, no details.
